attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a new array and type the image variable names inside the brackets [ ]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ What might the 6 image variables be used for in this project?

❓ What should be added inside the brackets of the colors array declaration?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In this project, the image variables will be used as matching cards. The Ninja is welcome to update the colors used with the fill tool in the paint editor; they should update the name of the image variable too, if so.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by reviewing the code already in the editor!


Notice that there are already 3 custom sprite kinds declared, 7 image variables created, and several code comments already in the editor.


Click on the palette to view each image variable. Notice that there is a cardBack image which will serve as the “card cover” and 6 solid colored variable images.


Underneath // array set up, use the keyword let to declare a new array called colors. Type an assignment operator and a pair of brackets [ ] with the image variable names typed inside, separated by commas. Do not include the cardBack variable in the array.


Now, the color images are stored in the colors array to be used in the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the concat function to duplicate the elements of the colors array so that the new colorCards array will contain 2 elements of each color?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the concat function used to duplicate the elements in the colors array?

❓ How might the colorCards and colorCardDeck arrays be used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡In this example, the concat function is used to  concatenate, or join, the elements of the colors array with the elements of the colors array. This action duplicates the elements of the colors array, storing 2 image variables of each color in colorCards.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider other ways they’ve joined values in JavaScript, such as using a plus sign + or the join function. Neither of these options will work in this instance because the elements in 2 arrays are being joined together, rather than individual string or number values.
steps.instructions:
Create a shuffled deck of cards with 2 of each color card!


Duplicate the values of the colors array in a new array. Use the keyword let to declare a new array called colorCards underneath // array set up. To the right of the assignment operator, type colors and a dot operator, then select the concat function from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses with colors typed inside.


The concat function concatenates, or joins, the values of 2 arrays. Here, the 6 elements of the colors array are duplicated to create a new array that contains all 12 elements. 


Use the keyword let to declare an empty array called colorCardDeck below the colorCards array. Since the colorCardDeck array will contain images, use : Image[] after its name. Then, type an assignment operator and a second pair of brackets [ ].

steps.hints: ❓Did you set randomIndex to a random index between 0 and the length of colorCards array minus 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the for loop and the randomIndex variable used to shuffle the colors from the colorCards array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic of the for loop code. The for loop will run 12 times, once for each element in the colorCards array. Each time the loop runs, a random index will be selected from the current length of the colorCards array.
steps.instructions:
Shuffle the order of colors before placing the images on the screen!


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath // game set up. Change the counter variable to count, then replace 5 with 12 in the run condition expression, so that the loop runs 12 times, once for each card in the array.


Inside the loop, use the keyword let to declare a randomIndex variable. Use randint to assign the variable a value between 0 and the length of the colorCards array minus 1.


Now, each time the loop runs, a random index will be selected from the 12 cards in the deck.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use push to add an element to the colorCardDeck array, and removeAt to take an element out of the colorCards array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it necessary to add the value stored in the randomIndex variable to the colorCardDeck array and remove it from the colorCards array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic of the for loop code. The for loop will run 12 times, once for each element in the colorCards array. Each time the loop runs, a random index will be selected from the current length of the colorCards array. The element at the selected index will then be pushed to colorCardDeck. Because a random value will be selected each time, this will create a “shuffled” order of values in colorCardDeck. The selected index needs to be removed from colorCards, so that no more than 2 of each color are placed in colorCardDeck.
steps.instructions:
Add each selected index to a new deck to shuffle the order of the cards!


Add the element at the randomIndex of the colorCards array to the colorCardDeck array. Inside the for loop, type colorCardDeck and a dot operator, then select push from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses with colorCards followed by a pair of brackets [ ] with randomIndex typed inside.


Remove the element at the randomIndex from the colorCards array. Type the name of the array followed by a dot operator. Select removeAt from the code completion tool, then type a pair of parentheses with randomIndex typed inside.


Now, each time the for loop runs, the element at a random index will be selected and removed from the colorCards array and added to the colorCardDeck array.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the pop function to remove and return the last element in the colorCardDeck array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How are the nested for loops used to create multiple Card sprites?

❓ What does the pop function do? How is it being used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In the nested for loops, the outer for loop will run 4 times. Each time the outer for loop runs, the inner for loop will run 3 times. Each time the inner for loop runs, it will create 3 new Card sprites. Once both for loops have finished running, 12 Card sprites will have been created.

💡 The pop function removes the last element from an array and returns it. In this example, each time a new Card sprite is created, its image is set to the last element in the colorCardDeck array. Because the pop function removes the last element, a new image will be used each time a new Card sprite is created.
steps.instructions:
Create a grid of Card sprites on screen!


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath the existing for loop under // game set up. Change the counter variable i to x in all 3 expressions, then replace 5 with 4 in the run condition expression, so that the loop runs 4 times. 


Drag another [for] inside the curly brackets of the for loop. Change the counter variable i to y in all 3 expressions, then replace 5 with 3 in the run condition expression, so that the loop runs 3 times.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets of the inner for loop. Change the sprite name to flippedCard, and the sprite kind to Card.


Replace the image parameter with colorCardDeck and type a dot operator. Select pop from the code completion tool and type a pair of parentheses. The pop function will remove and return the last element from an array.


Now, each time a Card sprite is created, its image will be set to the last element in the colorCardDeck array.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create 3 new variables that can be used in the x and y-position variable equations?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How are the 3 variables used to set each Card sprite’s x- and y-positions?

❓ Where will the 12 Card sprites appear on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic of the nested for loop’s code. Each time the outer for loop runs, the inner for loop will run 3 times. Each time the inner for loop runs, it will set the x and y-positions of the 3 new Card sprites. Each time the outer loop is run, 3 Card sprites will be placed in a column on the screen. This will repeat 4 times, placing a total of 12 Card sprites in 3 rows and 4 columns on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Position the shuffled Card sprites on screen!


Create 3 new variables to add spacing between each Card sprite and offset sprites from the edges of the screen. Under // game set up, create 3 variables: spacing, set to 25, xOffset, set to 18, and yOffset, set to 20.


Inside the nested for loops, declare cardX and cardY variables to set the x- and y- position of each Card sprite. Set each variable by multiplying the x or y counter variable by the sum of the flippedCard width or height and the spacing variable, placed inside parentheses. Add the value of xOffset or yOffset to the end of the equation to offset the sprites from the edges of the screen. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x(x) y(y)] inside the curly brackets of the inner for loop under the variable code. Update the sprite name to flippedCard then use the cardX and cardY position variablesas the x and y parameters.


Click ▶ to see 12 random Card sprites appear in a grid on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the push function to the cardArray inside the for loop, then type the flippedCard sprite name inside the parentheses?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of elements can be stored in the cardArray?

❓ Why might each Card sprite be added to the cardArray?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that an array can be made up of image, string, number, or sprite values. However, all elements in the array must be of the same type. As a result, it’s important to define what type of elements the empty array will store, so that the program is unable to add different types of elements into the same array.

💡 Each time a Card sprite is created, it will be pushed, or added, to the cardArray. This will be helpful for finding the index of each sprite and matching the images of multiple Card sprites later in the project.
steps.instructions:
Store the shuffled Card sprites in an array!


Under // array set up, use the keyword let to declare an empty array called cardArray. Since the cardArray will contain sprites, use : Sprite[] after its name. Type an assignment operator and a second pair of brackets [ ] 


Add each Card sprite to the cardArray as it is created. Underneath the code that creates a flippedCard sprite, type the name of the array followed by a dot operator. Select push from the code completion tool, then type a pair of parentheses with flippedCard inside.


Now, whenever a new Card sprite is created, its value will be added to the cardArray.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create the CardBack sprites and set their position inside the nested for loops?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where will the 12 CardBack sprites appear on screen?

❓ What color might the background be set to so that both the Card and CardBack sprites are visible?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the 12 CardBack sprites will be placed in the same positions as the Card sprites, so that the black images cover each random color.

💡 Point out to the ninja that they should select a background color that is different from any of the Card or CardBack sprite images, so that they are all visible on screen.
steps.instructions:
Position the CardBack sprites so that the Card sprites are “covered” on screen! 


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets of the inner for loop. Change the sprite name to unflippedCard, then replace the image parameter with cardBack and change the sprite kind to CardBack. 


Copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) the flippedCard position code on the line below the code that creates the CardBack sprites. Change the sprite name to unflippedCard but leave the x and y parameters the same. 


Change the background color so the black CardBack sprites can be seen on screen. Open Scene, drag [set background color to (color)] below the variable code under // game set up. Set the color parameter to a color not used for either the 6 Card sprites or the CardBack sprite.


Click ▶ to see CardBack sprites covering each Card sprite on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use setFlag to update the StayInScreen property so that the player doesn’t move off screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using the setFlag function to set a sprite to stay in screen different than using the setStayInScreen function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Previously in JavaScript, the ninja has used the setStayInScreen function to prevent a sprite from moving off screen. They can also use the setFlag function, which offers a list of many different sprite flags, to code a sprite to stay in screen. This function uses the StayInScreen function as a parameter.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // game set up. Select a Player sprite image and update the sprite name.


Allow the Player sprite to move around the screen. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the sprite creation code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name.


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath the Player sprite movement code. Update the sprite name, then change the flag parameter to SpriteFlag.StayInScreen and the on parameter to true.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite move around the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the z property to the correct depth so the Card, CardBack, and Player sprites appear in the correct order on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might the depth level of the Card and CardBack sprites need to be set?

❓ Why is the Player sprite assigned a greater z value than the Card or CardBack sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the z property can be used to set the order in which sprites appear on the screen. The Card sprites have a lower z-position value so they will appear below the CardBack sprites. This allows the Card sprites to appear “hidden”. 

💡 The Player sprite is assigned a greater z-position value than the Card and CardBack sprites so that it always appears in front of the other sprites. The Card sprite has a z-position value of 1, CardBack, 2, and the Player sprite, 4. In the next step, the Card sprite will be “flipped”, revealing its color and will be assigned a z-position value of 3, so that it appears in front of the CardBack sprite, but below the Player sprite.
steps.instructions:
Set the depth levels for the Card, CardBack, and Player sprites so they appear in the correct order on screen.


Use different depth levels to make the CardBack sprites appear in front of the Card sprites until they are “flipped over”. Inside the nested for loops, type the names of the flippedCard and unflippedCard sprites followed by a dot operator. Select the z property from the code completion tool then type an assignment operator. Set the flippedCard sprite to 1 and the unflippedCard sprite to 2 so the Card sprite appears below the CardBack sprite.


Set the Player sprite to always appear on top. Type the name of the Player sprite followed by a dot operator. Select the z property from the code completion tool, then type an assignment operator and the number 4.


Click ▶ to see how the depth changes how the sprites appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use brackets to access an element from the cardArray, then use a dot operator to update the z-position of that sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the Player sprite overlaps with a Card sprite?

❓ What value will be assigned to the arrayIndex variable?

❓ Why should the value at the arrayIndex of the cardArray be assigned 3 as its z-position?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps with a Card sprite, the Card sprite’s kind will be changed to Player. The program will find the index of the Card sprite in the cardArray, then bring that Card sprite to the front, above the CardBack sprite, so that its color is visible.

💡 The sprite at the  arrayIndex of the cardArray should be assigned 3 as its z-position so that it appears in front of the CardBack sprite, but below the Player sprite.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the Player sprite overlaps with a Card sprite!


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // game events. Change the otherKind parameter to Card. 


Change the Card sprite’s kind to prevent repeat overlapping. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) kind to (value)] inside the onOverlap event’s curly brackets. Replace mySprite with otherSprite and use the default value SpriteKind.Player.


Find the index of the overlapped sprite. Use the keyword let to declare a new variable called arrayIndex. To the right of the assignment operator, type cardArray and a dot operator. Select indexOf, then type a pair of parentheses with otherSprite typed inside.


Bring the Card sprite to the front. Type cardArray followed by a set of brackets with arrayIndex inside. Type a dot operator and select z, then add an assignment operator and assign it a value of 3, so that the Card sprite now appears in front of the CardBack sprite on screen.


Click ▶ to see the color of the Card sprite be revealed on overlap with the Player sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the push function to the flippedCards array name inside the if conditional, and type arrayIndex inside the parentheses?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of elements can be stored in the flippedCards array?

❓ When will the value stored in the arrayIndex variable be added to the flippedCards array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that an array can be made up of image, string, number, or sprite values. However, all elements in the array must be of the same type. As a result, it’s important to define what type of elements the empty array will store, so that the program is unable to add different types of elements into the same array.

💡 Each time a Player sprite overlaps a Card sprite, if the length of the flippedCards array is less than 2, the Card sprite’s value will be pushed to the flippedCards array. This action prevents more than 2 Card sprites from being “flipped” at once, because each Card sprite’s sprite kind is changed once “flipped”.
steps.instructions:
Allow only 2 Card sprites to be flipped over at a time.


Use the keyword let to declare a new empty array called flippedCards under // array set up. Since the flippedCards array will contain numbers, use : number[] after its name. Then, type an assignment operator and a second pair of brackets [ ]


Open Logic and drag [if] inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event. Cut (Ctrl + X) all of the existing code in the onOverlap event and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the curly brackets of the if condition. Replace true with code that checks if the length of the flippedCards array is less than 2.


Add the arrayIndex of the overlapped card to flippedCards. Inside the conditional, type flippedCards and a dot operator. Select push, then type a pair of parentheses with arrayIndex inside.


Click ▶ to see how many Card sprites appear at a time!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create 2 new variables and assign them the values of elements at index 0 and 1 of the flippedCards array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What values will be stored in the 2 variables? What types of values are they?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic of the variable code. When there are 2 Card sprites “flipped”, the index values of the 2 Card sprites will be stored in the firstCard and secondCard variables. Because their number values have already been pushed to the flippedCards array, the variable can find them by using their index values.
steps.instructions:
Store the values of the Card sprites in variables to compare them!


Open Logic and drag another [if] inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event. Inside the parentheses, add code to check if the length of the flippedCards array is equal to 2. 


Inside the curly brackets of the if condition, use the keyword let to declare firstCard and secondCard variables. To the right of each assignment operator, type cardArray followed by a pair of brackets.


Inside the brackets for firstCard, type flippedCards[0] Repeat the process and use  index 1 for secondCard to access the values pushed to the flippedCards array when the Player sprite overlaps the 2 Card sprites.


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] below the variable code. Set the parameter to 1000, so that the project pauses briefly after the values of the flipped Card sprites have been stored.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a Boolean AND operator && and an inequality operator ! to check if the length of the flippedCards array is equal to 2 AND the checkingMatch variable is false?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When will the project store the values of the Card sprites in the firstCard and secondCard variables?

❓ Why is the checkingMatch variable necessary in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps 2 Card sprites and checkingMatch is false, the project will set checkingMatch to true then store the values of the Card sprites in the firstCard and secondCard variables. 

💡 The checkingMatch variable enables the project to only check if the images of the 2 Card sprites match when 2 Card sprites have been “flipped” and if the project is not currently checking for matches.
steps.instructions:
Set when the project can and cannot check if the images of the “flipped” Card sprites match!


Use the keyword let to declare a new Boolean variable called checkingMatch below the other code under // game set up. Assign a false value to the variable, so that the project cannot check for matches yet.


Inside the parentheses of the second if statement, add a Boolean AND operator && and an inequality operator ! to check if the checkingMatch variable is false. If both conditions are true, set the checkingMatch variable to true inside the if conditional, so that the project is able to check if the 2 images match.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a conditional to check if firstCard.image is equal to secondCard.image, and use setKind to change both sprite kinds to Match?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the code inside the conditional check if the images of the 2 Card sprites match?

❓ Why are the sprite kinds of the 2 variables changed to Match?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk through the logic of the conditional with the ninja. When the length of the flippedCards array is equal to 2 AND checkingMatch is false, the project will check to see if the colors of the 2 Card sprites are the same. This can be done by comparing the image properties of the 2 sprites to check for equality. 

💡 If the images of the 2 Card sprites are the same, then their sprite kinds will be changed to Match. This prevents the Card sprites from triggering a future overlap event.
steps.instructions:
Check if the image of the first Card sprite is equal to the image of the second Card sprite!


Open Logic and drag [if else] inside the curly brackets of the second if condition in the onOverlap event. Replace true with code that uses the image property to check if the firstCard image is equal to the secondCard image.


Change both variable’s sprite kinds if the 2 images are the same. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) kind to (value)] inside the if condition’s curly brackets 2 times. Replace mySprite with the variable names and change the sprite kinds to SpriteKind.Match


Now, if the 2 Card sprite images are the same, their sprite kinds will be changed to Match and they will no longer be part of game play.

steps.hints: ❓Did you reset the firstCard and secondCard‘s z properties and sprite kinds if the images do not match?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the depth level of each Card sprite reset, if their images do not match?

❓ Why are the sprite kinds of the 2 “flipped” Card sprites reset to Card, if their images do not match?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think of a “memory match” game that they’ve played previously. If the player flips over 2 cards and they are a match, they are typically added to a separate pile or a “score”. If they are not a match, they are turned over for the next turn. Prompt the ninja to make the connection between this type of game and the project they are building. In this example, the depth level is used to “return” the non-matching cards so they are able to be selected in the next round.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that the 2 Card sprites’ kinds are immediately changed to Player once they are “flipped”. By changing their sprite kinds to Card, the sprites are “returned” to the game and are able to be selected again.
steps.instructions:
Hide the Card sprites if the 2 images do not match.


Reset each Card sprite’s depth level if the 2 images do not match. Inside the curly brackets of the else condition, set both the firstCard and secondCard z-positions to 1. 


Copy (Ctrl + C) the setKind code from the if condition and paste (Ctrl + V) it below the z-position code in the else condition. Change both sprite kinds back to Card.


Click ▶ to see the Card sprites be covered by the CardBack sprites if the 2 images do not match.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the flippedCards array to empty, and reassign checkingMatch to false ?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the values of the flippedCards array and the checkingMatch variable be reset once the project has checked for a match?

❓ What symbols should be used to assign an empty array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The values of flippedCards and checkingMatch should be reset once the project has checked for a match so that the next time a Player sprite overlaps 2 Card sprites, the project can accurately check again. If their values are not reset, the index values of the variables and the array will not be aligned and the project will be unable to accurately check for a match.

💡 Explain to the ninja that by typing an assignment operator and a pair of brackets to the right of an array’s name, it clears out the elements in the array and resets it.
steps.instructions:
Reset the game so the user can select 2 different cards!


Underneath the closing bracket of the else condition, type flippedCards


﻿ Assign flippedCards to an empty array by typing an assignment operator and an empty pair of brackets. 


On the line below, assign a false value to checkingMatch, so that the code will not check for a match until 2 more cards are “flipped”.


Now, the values of flippedCards and checkingMatch will be reset so that the user can continue playing.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use setLifeImage to update the life meter image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many lives might the Player sprite begin the project with? 

❓ How many lives might the Player sprite gain or lose, depending on if the 2 images match?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The Ninja can add the setLifeImage function under // game set up to customize the life value image. Encourage the ninja to select an 8x8 image that fits the “life” for the Player sprite.
steps.instructions:
Gain or lose a life depending on if the 2 images match!


Open Info and drag [set life to (3)] underneath the variable code under // game set up. Update the value parameter to set how many lives the Player sprite will start the project with. 


Open Info again and drag [change life by (-1)] inside both the if and else conditions. Change the value parameter in the if condition to a positive number and keep the value parameter in the else condition set to a negative number.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite gain or lose a life depending on whether the 2 images match!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the allOfKind function to check if there are 12 Match sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the project check if there are 12 Match sprites in order to end the game?

❓ What does the allOfKind function do? How is it being used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that there are 2 Card sprites for each of the 6 colors on screen. If 12 Match sprites have been created, that means that the Player sprite has matched all the sprites of the same color, winning the game.

💡 The allOfKind function returns an array of all the sprites of the given kind. This function is used to check for the length of the array of all Match sprites on screen to trigger the game to end.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the  setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
End the game once the Player sprite has found all of the matches!


Open Logic and drag [if] underneath the checkingMatch = false code. 


Replace true with code that checks if there are 12 Match sprites. Open Sprites and drag [array of sprites of kind (kind)] inside the parentheses of the conditional. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

sprites.allOfKind(SpriteKind.Player)

The allOfKind function takes 1 parameter: kind. Change the kind parameter to SpriteKind.Match. Type a dot operator after the closing parenthesis to select the length property, then an equality operator and the number 12. Now, the conditional will check if 12 Match sprites have been created.


Open Game and drag [game over (true)] inside the curly brackets of the conditional. Keep the win parameter set to true and add an effect, too. 


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Memory Match
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses index values and empty arrays to create a color matching game!

validationItems.text: Store 6 image variables in a colors array.
Use the concat function to create a colorCards array containing two of each color variable.
Create an empty colorCardDeck Image array to hold the shuffled cards.
Shuffle the card images and store them in the empty colorCardDeck array.
Use nested for loops and spacing variables to place the cards in a grid.
Store the Card sprites in a cardArray.
Create and place 12 CardBack sprites on top of the Card sprites.
Add a player sprite, move it with the controller, and set it to stay in the screen.
Set the z-positions for the Card, CardBack, and Player sprites.
Change a Card sprite’s z-position and SpriteKind when it overlaps with the Player sprite.
Create a flippedCards array and allow only 2 cards to be flipped at a time.
If there are two flipped cards, store them in firstCard and secondCard variables.
Use the checkingMatch variable to track when the game is checking for a match.
If the two flipped card images match, set their sprite kinds to Match.
If the two flipped card images do not match, set their sprite kinds to Card and set their z-position to 1.
After checking for a match, set the checkingMatch variable to false and set the value of flippedCards to an empty array.
Increase and decrease the player’s lives based on if the cards match.
End the game when there are 12 Match sprites.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about arrays and array functions. You’ll build on your understanding of arrays in JavaScript by exploring functions that will help you access, modify, and join elements in an array. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Push It, Pop It, Join It, Concat It!
badges.description: Use several different array functions in JavaScript to access and modify the data stored inside an array.

badges.title: A String of Numbers
badges.description: Use the toString function to convert a number to a string

badges.title: Arrays All The Way Down
badges.description: Create a nested array in JavaScript.

badges.title: Joined at the Hip
